title: A water drop that freezes from the outside in can explode

cover.alt: High-speed close-up of a freezing water drop bursting: shards of ice fly up and away beside an intact drop on the left.

body: Water expands as it turns to ice. When a supercooled drop starts to freeze, a shell of ice forms on the outside first and thickens inwards, trapping the liquid still inside. As that water freezes and tries to expand, pressure builds: the shell cracks, flakes break off, and finally the whole drop bursts, throwing out fragments at about 1.5 metres per second. Physicists at the University of Twente caught it on high-speed video and published the result in 2017.

slides.alt: Slow-motion close-up of two small water drops on a surface. The right-hand drop, under a pointed tip, is freezing over; suddenly it bursts into flying shards of ice, while the left-hand drop stays whole.
slides.caption: In slow motion: a drop freezing under the tip that started it suddenly bursts into shards of ice. The drop on the left stays whole.

steps.label: A touch of silver iodide starts the freezing
An ice shell forms and thickens inwards
Water trapped inside expands as it freezes
The shell cracks, and then the drop explodes

left.label: Molten glass
left.text: Dropped into cold water, it hardens from the outside in and shrinks, which makes the glass bead very strong.

right.label: Water
right.text: It expands as it freezes inside its own ice shell, so the pressure keeps building until the drop bursts.

slides.heading: It happens in clouds too
slides.text: Meteorologists know that drops explode like this in the cold tops of clouds. These bursts can help start precipitation, and can quickly turn a cloud of liquid droplets into a cloud of ice.

slides.question: How did physicists at the University of Twente make their drops cold enough to freeze?
options: Let them evaporate in a vacuum
Put them in a kitchen freezer
slides.explanation: The drops sat on a water-repellent surface in a vacuum chamber, where evaporation cooled them below zero without freezing them, until a silver iodide tip set the ice off.
